newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan corporate sentiment worsens unexpectedly.
newsitem.headline: Japan corporate sentiment worsens unexpectedly.

text.p: Corporate Japan grew unexpectedly gloomy in August, with a key index in a Bank of Japan quarterly survey released on Wednesday defying most predictions by sliding further into negative territory.

Analysts said the figure removed fears of an interest rate increase but could be negative for Japanese stocks. The survey results were announced just as the stock market closed for its lunch break but yields on Japanese government bonds fell and the dollar gained more than half a yen to 108.30 by midday.

The diffusion index for major manufacturers in the Bank of Japan's quarterly corporate survey, or "tankan", fell to minus seven in August from minus three in May, when the previous survey was conducted.
The tankan is closely watched by financial markets as a clue to future monetary policy.
The index represents the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those who expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.

Despite speculation as recently as last month that the Bank of Japan might soon tighten its super-easy credit policy -- in place for nearly a year -- most economists had said that the central bank was unlikely to move yet, given worries that Japan's economic recovery might lose steam later in the year.

Commenting on the survey result, Kiyoshi Kimura, general manager of the research department at Societe Generale Securities Ltd, said: "It was lower than the market's consensus. Expectations of a rate hike will completely disappear. But it would be a negative factor to the stock market."
Kenneth Courtis, chief economist, Deutsche Capital Markets, said the picture was mixed.

"The DI (diffusion index) isn't very good...but the other numbers are actually pretty good. My feeling is you've just got a little pause in the economy...and that we're going to be clicking back into gear."

Andrew Shipley, chief economist at Schroders Japan, said: "The headline numbers are quite bad but I don't think they are pointing to recession...and we should see continued growth in upcoming quarters."
"There are disturbing trends in the manufacturing sector, that the next tankan will not reach expectations."

Most economists surveyed by Reuters had expected that the major manufacturers' diffusion index would rise somewhat, with forecasts ranging from minus four to plus five. Seven out of 15 think tanks had predicted that the index would edge into positive territory.
